--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.disjoint_union()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Compute the disjoint union of this graph with another graph. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.disjoint_union()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Compute the disjoint union of this graph with another graph. title: >- [Graph.disjoint_union()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Compute the disjoint union of this graph with another graph. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the disjoint union of this graph with another graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L49926-L50024){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.disjoint_union(other) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Disjoint union](../assets/graphs/disjoint-union.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="G is a triangle on nodes 1, 2, 3 (accent); H is a single edge between its own nodes 1 and 2 (teal). The disjoint union never merges ids: H's nodes are renumbered 4 and 5, giving five nodes in two separate components." width="100%"} Combines graphs by renumbering the other graph's nodes to avoid conflicts. The resulting graph has all nodes and edges from both, with no overlap. The nodes of the calling graph keep their IDs, while every node of `other=` is shifted up by the largest node ID in the calling graph (so with IDs `1` to `3` in the calling graph, `other=`'s node `1` becomes `4`). Edges from `other=` are remapped to the new IDs. Because no node is ever shared, no edge can link the two parts and the result always has at least as many components as the two inputs combined. This is useful for: - assembling a multi-component graph from independently built pieces - putting several networks side by side so one algorithm call covers all of them - building test graphs with a known number of components Neither input is modified; a new `Graph` is returned. If you want nodes with matching IDs to be treated as the same node, use `union()` instead. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The graph to combine with this one. It must have the same directedness as the calling graph. Its nodes are renumbered as described above, and any of its labels that already exist in the calling graph get a numeric suffix (`"A"` becomes `"A_2"`, or `"A_3"` if `"A_2"` is also taken). If either graph is weighted, the result is weighted. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph with both graphs combined disjointly: the node count is the sum of both node counts and the edge count is the sum of both edge counts. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graphs have different directedness. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Rather than merging on shared node IDs the way `union()` does, `disjoint_union()` renumbers the incoming graph so its IDs sit strictly above the highest ID in the calling graph. Node and edge attributes carry through unchanged. Labels do too, unless one clashes with a label already in the calling graph: labels must be unique, so the incoming one gets a numeric suffix (`"A"` becomes `"A_2"`). The result is a graph with two provably disjoint components, or more when several calls are chained, which is a handy way to assemble a multi-component graph out of independent pieces. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~union`) : Combine two graphs, matching nodes by ID. [](`~full_join`) : Combine two graphs and join every pair across them. [](`~disjoint_union_all`) : Combine any number of graphs, keeping their nodes apart. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Node IDs are never merged: the other graph's nodes get new IDs, so two triangles stay separate. A label that's already taken gets a suffix, so the second graph's "A" becomes "A_2": ::: {#638d7521 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g1 = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) g1.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) both = g1.disjoint_union(g1) labels = both.get_node_df()["label"].to_list() both.count_weakly_connected_components(), labels ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (2, ['A', 'B', 'C', 'A_2', 'B_2', 'C_2']) ``` ::: ::: ### Two towns `ec.friends()` is a network of friendships among the 24 members of a chess club and a climbing club. Suppose a second town has clubs with the same members' names and the same friendships. Their disjoint union keeps the towns apart, 48 people and 86 friendships, and the second town's people get a suffix: ::: {#e9baffa5 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} towns = ec.friends().disjoint_union(ec.friends()) towns.count_nodes(), towns.count_edges(), towns.get_label_from_id(25) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (48, 86, 'Ada_2') ``` ::: ::: ::: {#816b8d7d .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} towns.plot(color_by="club", show_labels=False, seed=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: `union()` would instead match the two graphs node for node and give back a single town.
